problem: It says 99.9% availability in a 30-day month allows 'at most 43 minutes' of downtime, but the formula right below gives 43.2 minutes. The two numbers do not match, and a student copying 43 into an answer loses marks.
fix: Write: 'For example, 99.9% availability in a 30-day month allows 43.2 minutes of downtime (about 43 minutes).'

where: Section 3, the four bullet points after the formula
problem: The list appears with no lead-in sentence, and it mixes billing meters (compute, storage, managed database) with a software stack (OpenStack). A reader can take OpenStack as a fourth thing that is billed.
fix: Add a lead-in such as 'Common billed items and one stack you will meet:' and label OpenStack as a stack, not a meter, or move it out of the list.

problem: The text says the carrier links the consumer's network to the provider's edge, but the figure has only one carrier edge, carrier to provider, so the consumer side of the link is not drawn. The text also says the broker aggregates provider catalogues, yet no edge runs from provider to broker.
fix: Add a carrier-to-consumer edge (or label the carrier node 'links consumer to provider edge') and add a provider-to-broker edge labelled 'catalogue'.

problem: The terms 'GB-month' and 'egress' are used without definition. A first-time reader may not know that GB-month means one GB stored for one month, or that egress means data leaving the provider.
fix: Define both where they first appear: 'a GB-month is one GB stored for one month' and 'egress is data moved out of the provider to the internet or another network'.
